explain: Types: every variable has a type written before its name (int, double, char). The type says how much memory it uses.
remember: Type first, then name: int age.

explain: Statements end in ; and blocks are { }. A program is statements inside functions; it starts at main.
Functions: return type, name, (typed parameters), then a block. A function must be written (or declared) before it is used.
remember: Same shape as main: type name(params) { }.

explain: Pointers: & gives the address of a variable, * follows an address to the value. This is how C shares and changes memory.
example: Arrays, strings and changing values in functions.

explain: An array is many values of one type in a row; nums[i] is really *(nums + i), a pointer step.
remember: Array = pointer to the first one.

explain: A struct groups variables of different types under one name. Read the parts with a dot.
example: A point, a person, a record.
remember: struct = my own type made from types.

explain: A string in C is an array of char that ends with a hidden \0.
remember: C string = char array + \0 at the end.

explain: #include brings in a header file. Every C program starts in main. \n is a new line.
example: The start of every C program.

explain: int for whole numbers, char for one character, float for decimals. printf fills %d %c %f in order.
example: Storing a score, a letter grade, and a price.

explain: Start at 0, keep going while i < 3, add 1 each time.
example: Going through every item in an array.

explain: A function says what type it returns (int) and the type of each input.
example: Splitting a program into small named steps.

explain: &x is the address of x. int *p holds an address. *p reaches the value at that address.
example: Letting a function change a variable it was given.

explain: malloc asks for memory; free gives it back. Every malloc needs a free.
example: Arrays whose size you only know while the program runs.

explain: struct groups related values into one new type.
example: A point on screen, or a player with name and score.

explain: A string is an array of chars. string.h has helpers like strlen.
printf placeholders: %d whole number, %f decimal, %.2f two decimals, %c one letter, %s text.
scanf reads typed input. & gives scanf the address to store it in.

syntax:
char name[50];
fgets(name, sizeof name, stdin);
explain: fgets reads a whole line safely, never more than the size of the array.
int whole numbers, float/double decimals (double is more exact), char one character.
example: Choosing the right box for each value.

syntax:
#include <stdbool.h>
bool done = false;
explain: C has no true/false built in; stdbool.h adds bool, true, false.

syntax:
#define MAX_USERS 100
const double PI = 3.14159;
explain: #define replaces a name with a value before compiling. const makes a variable read-only.
Run different code for different cases.
switch picks a case by number or char. break stops it falling into the next case.

syntax: int max = (a > b) ? a : b;
explain: condition ? ifTrue : ifFalse in one line.
while repeats as long as the condition is true.
example: Reading until the end of a file.

explain: do-while always runs at least once, then checks.
example: Asking until the input is valid.

explain: continue skips to the next round, break stops the loop.
An array holds many values of one type. sizeof math gives how many.
A 2D array is rows and columns. grid[row][column].
Text is an array of char ending with '\0'. strlen length, strcat join, strcmp gives 0 when equal.
strcpy copies text. snprintf writes formatted text into an array safely.
atoi turns text into int, atof into double.
A prototype lets you use a function before its full code.
example: Putting main at the top of the file.

explain: Recursion: a function that calls itself, with a case that stops it.
static keeps a local variable's value between calls.
example: Counting how many times a function ran.

explain: Pass addresses so a function can change the caller's variables.
example: Functions that need to return two things.

explain: An array name is a pointer to its first item. p + 2 moves two items forward.

syntax:
int *p = NULL;
if (p != NULL) printf("%d\n", *p);
explain: NULL means "points to nothing". Always check before using a pointer.
calloc makes memory filled with zeros. realloc makes it bigger. free gives it back.
typedef lets you write Person instead of struct Person.

syntax:
Person *ptr = &p;
ptr->age = 37;
explain: -> reaches a field through a pointer. Same as (*ptr).age.
example: Changing a record inside a function.

explain: enum gives names to numbers (RED=0, GREEN=1, BLUE=2).
fopen opens a file ("w" write, "r" read, "a" append). Always fclose it.
Read a file one line at a time.
argc is how many words were typed, argv holds them. argv[0] is the program.
(double) changes a type. Without it, 7 / 2 is 3 (whole-number division).
+= adds to itself, % remainder, & bitwise AND, << shift left (times 2).
srand seeds the generator with the time; rand() % 6 + 1 gives 1 to 6.

syntax:
#include <math.h>
printf("%.2f %.2f\n", sqrt(16.0), pow(2, 10));
explain: math.h has sqrt, pow, and more. Compile with -lm on Linux.
A header lists functions for other files. The #ifndef guard stops it being included twice.

syntax:
gcc -Wall -o main main.c
./main
gcc -g main.c utils.c -o app
explain: -Wall shows warnings, -o names the program, -g adds debug info. List several .c files to join them.
